value: pinealectomized and control cavefish were both more active in the light and less active in the dark
eye: whole animal (juvenile Pachon cave morph, pinealectomized and control)
method: behavioural: locomotor activity in the day (light) and night (dark) phases of a 13:11 h light:dark cycle, one 24 h recording per fish analysed at ZT6-10 and ZT19-23; pinealectomy compared with sham controls
conditions: Pachon cave morph (laboratory-raised descendants of fish collected from Cueva de El Pachon, Tamaulipas, Mexico; about 10-15 laboratory generations); juveniles 6 to 16 weeks; light 30 to 100 lux; the paired day-night comparisons give N = 18 control (t17 = 3.9) and N = 15 pinealectomized (t14 = 3.8) cavefish, P < 0.01 after Bonferroni correction. The section's final paragraph restates the same comparison as P = 0.005 (control) and P = 0.008 (pinealectomized) ('As reported, a diurnal activity shift was observed ...'). Light and dark are the day and night of an entrained 13:11 L:D cycle in the same fish, with no constant-dark or constant-light condition, so a direct light response (masking) is not separated from a circadian rhythm; the Discussion says the light-ON burst could also be regulated by circadian rhythm without light input. White LED; 1.2 to 1.5 cm SL; individual wells 3.48 cm across, which the Discussion says may make fish nervous and induce unexpected responses. Cavefish juvenile eyes are mostly degenerated but not absent, so the paper's data do not by themselves show the light response is non-ocular; the paper concludes the pineal contributes little to light-dependent basal activity in either morph (null for a pineal role).

value: female ABR thresholds were significantly lower than male thresholds from 0.2 to 1.1 kHz, except at 0.9 kHz (p = 0.053); the authors note waveforms were not obvious at or above 1.1 kHz
method: electrophysiological: auditory brainstem response to tone bursts, females compared with males
conditions: 10 males and 10 females, all 5 years old, bought from farms in Hainan Province and kept at 28-32 degrees C before testing (testing temperature not separately stated); females were the larger sex (the tool read gave mean body mass 1681.6 g against 1069.7 g for males); tone-burst thresholds were generally about 3 dB lower in females across 0.2-1.1 kHz (p < 0.05), so the sex difference is small; at 0.9 kHz female thresholds were still lower but not significantly; tympanum diameter did not differ significantly between the sexes (p = 0.08, n = 10 per sex), and the authors say the difference 'does not appear' related to tympanum size; females were also about 57% heavier, so a body-size effect is not excluded; airborne sound; animals anaesthetized for recording (one tool read: sodium pentobarbital); tone bursts 0.2 to 1.5 kHz in 100 Hz steps; dB SPL with no stated reference, free-field calibration at the jaw tip

method: electrophysiological: auditory brainstem response to tone bursts; hearing range as stated by the authors
conditions: Lowest thresholds about 40 dB SPL at 0.6 kHz in females and 45 dB SPL at 0.6 kHz in males (best frequency 600 Hz). 10 males and 10 females, 5 years old, held at 28-32 degrees C before testing; anaesthetized; airborne sound. Tone bursts 0.2 to 1.5 kHz were tested; the Results say waveforms were not obvious at or above 1.1 kHz, and the Discussion gives the range as 0.2 to 0.9 kHz. Test temperature is not stated (animals held at 28-32 degrees C before testing); in this subspecies the ABR bandwidth depends on temperature (Wang et al. 2022, on main: 0.2-0.5 kHz at 10 degrees C to 0.2-1.5 kHz at 40 degrees C), so the range applies at an unstated temperature.

method: behavioural: playback of substrate vibration through a buried tactile transducer, calling activity of wild males
